title: Trezor Brevo Breach Exposed 347,000 Emails to Phishing Attack
excerpt: A flaw in email provider Brevo's login system let attackers send phishing emails from Trezor's own domain to 347,000 newsletter subscribers — the hardware wallet maker's second third-party data breach in weeks.
body:
• Trezor said a September 9 breach at its email provider Brevo exposed roughly 347,000 newsletter email addresses and enabled a phishing campaign sent from Trezor's own domain.
  • The phishing email, titled "Critical Security Alert: STM32 Entropy Vulnerability," asked recipients to download an app and enter their wallet backup password; Trezor disabled the malicious domain within 20 minutes, but about 2,500 people had already clicked it.
  • Brevo said attackers exploited a flaw in its SAML single-sign-on handling to reach 138 client accounts; hardware wallet maker BitBox and portfolio tracker CoinTracking confirmed their customers were also targeted.
  • No Trezor products, wallets, or account systems were affected. The incident is the second third-party breach to hit Trezor customers in weeks, following the August breach at shipping partner ShipMonk.

Hardware crypto wallet maker Trezor is warning customers for the second time in as many months that a company it relies on was hacked, exposing customer data to attackers. The company confirmed this week that a cyberattack on Brevo, the marketing platform it uses to send newsletters, allowed hackers to send roughly 347,000 phishing emails that appeared to come from Trezor itself — a supply-chain attack that turned Trezor's trusted sender identity into the weapon.

Context & Background

On September 9, 2026, Trezor said an unauthorized actor gained access to Brevo's system and used it to send emails from Trezor's own account. The phishing messages, sent to the company's opt-in newsletter database, carried the subject line "Critical Security Alert: STM32 Entropy Vulnerability" and warned of a supposed hardware-level flaw in the STM32 microcontrollers used in Trezor devices — one that, the emails claimed, could expose wallet seed phrases to brute-force attacks.

Recipients were urged to click a link, download an app, and enter their wallet backup password. With a stolen wallet backup, an attacker can irreversibly drain funds on the public blockchain. Trezor said it took down the phishing domain at the DNS level within 20 minutes, which disabled the link — but about 2,500 people had clicked it before the takedown.

"Please be aware that the email named 'Critical Security Alert: STM32 Entropy Vulnerability' is not coming from us, and it's a phishing attempt. Do not click on any link."

— Trezor, in a statement posted on X

Brevo's own postmortem, published September 10, explains the entry point: attackers exploited a flaw in Brevo's SAML single-sign-on handling, created an account, enabled SSO, and invited legitimate Brevo users into the configuration. Access should have been confined to the attackers' organization, but an authorization boundary failed — Brevo said the access was "not properly scoped" and "wrongly granted" to every organization the invited users could reach. In total, 138 Brevo accounts were accessed; six were used to send phishing emails, contacts were exported from 43, and 93 showed no meaningful activity.

Trezor was not the only crypto company hit. BitBox, the Swiss hardware wallet maker, reported a matching campaign impersonating it on the same day, and crypto portfolio tracker CoinTracking confirmed phishing emails were sent to its subscribers as well. Trezor stressed that the Brevo account stored only opt-in newsletter email addresses and no other customer data: "No other Trezor system was touched," the company said, adding that it had suspended the Brevo account to stop further email distribution.

Impact & Analysis

The campaign was unusually convincing because the emails came from Trezor's own domain and passed normal email authentication checks — the exact property that makes sender-trust so fragile. This is not an isolated pattern for the company. In August, Trezor alerted customers that shipping partner ShipMonk was breached, exposing names, phone numbers, email addresses, and postal addresses of at least 81,000 hardware buyers — and Trezor later disclosed that an additional 67,000 U.S. customers were affected. In January 2024, its third-party support ticketing portal was hacked, with names, usernames, and email addresses stolen from roughly 66,000 users.

For wallet owners, the guidance is narrow and absolute. Trezor says it never asks customers for their wallet backups — not by email, not through an app, not on any website. Treat any message demanding an urgent device update or wallet backup as hostile, even from a legitimate domain; verify warnings by navigating to trezor.io directly instead of clicking links, use a dedicated email address for crypto accounts, and distrust urgency — "critical security alert" language exists to short-circuit the checks that would expose the fraud.

"These addresses might be potentially used for other phishing attacks in the future. No other Trezor system was touched."

— Trezor, in its incident blog post

The 2,500 people who clicked before the takedown are the immediate concern: anyone who entered a wallet backup should move their funds to a newly generated wallet. And because the attackers walked away with 347,000 email addresses, Trezor expects more phishing built on this list in the coming weeks.

Diaspora Angle

Crypto ownership runs deep in the Indian diaspora, and hardware wallets are common among investors who self-custody. If you hold crypto on a Trezor, BitBox, or any hardware wallet, scrutinize every vendor-branded email in your inbox this week — and warn family members who may be less tuned in to phishing tactics.

What's Next

Trezor said it is reevaluating its relationships with vendors — a pointed commitment given that its recent incidents trace to third parties rather than its own infrastructure. Watch for Brevo's full remediation of its authorization boundary, and for follow-on phishing waves targeting the stolen address lists. The wallets remain uncompromised, but the human layer around them is now the attack surface that matters.
